newsitem.title: USA: US industry demand off but recession not seen - NABE.
newsitem.headline: US industry demand off but recession not seen - NABE.

text.p: Industrial demand looks to have suffered its sharpest slowdown in at least 15 years in the third quarter, but that is not a harbinger of recession, the National Association of Business Economists (NABE) said.

The group said on Tuesday that its quarterly survey of 104 members found that the growth of demand weakened across all industries last quarter, with retailers and wholesalers reporting an actual contraction in their business. Inflationary pressures also moderated.
"A significant slowdown occured in the third quarter," the association said.

NABE said that its index of industrial demand -- which compares the number of companies reporting a rise in business against those reporting a fall -- suffered its biggest tumble since its quarterly survey began in 1982.
Association President Mark Dadd noted though that the third quarter slowdown came on the heels of very rapid growth in the second quarter, when the economy expanded at a 4.7 percent annualized pace.
"We're still talking about continuing, but moderate, growth," he told Reuters.

Less than three percent of the economists surveyed think the economy will fall into recession next year. The rest expect the economy to continue to expand, although 45 percent said growth next year will be sluggish.

Reflecting that outlook, employers have turned more cautious about taking on new workers, the association said. More companies than not now expect to cut payrolls over the next six months, although most anticipate making no change.
The association said that businesses continue to run into difficulties in raising prices.
Over 75 percent of the firms that tried to raise prices in the third quarter were forced to either partially roll back the increases or totally rescind them.
Dadd, who is also chief economist for AT&T Corp, said he expects corporate profits to be "squeezed a bit" by the tough competitive environment.
Almost half of those surveyed reported shortages of skilled labor last quarter. The vast majority though said that wages and salaries remained unchanged during the period.
